thread.title: Battle over as Astoria plans pay out By INCE|Connect

author: INCE|Connect
title: Battle over as Astoria plans pay out By INCE|Connect
text:
© Reuters. RECM has agreed to call off its voluntary offer to minorities in light of Astoria Investments' proposed capital pay-out.
Astoria plans to sell all of its liquid investments and return cash to shareholders due to little prospect of its portfolio reflecting its true value in the short to medium term.
The global investment company says it has the buy-in of major shareholder RECM and Calibre (RECM), which has agreed to call off a voluntary offer to the group's minorities.
Astoria listed three years ago at R14.23 and, after briefly topping R18, its shares have traded below its listing price since. In late 2016, they were worth less than R10. Over the past six months, it said its shares had traded in a range of between R11.10 and R13.60, representing a discount range of about 29% to 15% to its net asset value (NAV) of $1.12 on 30 November. Its NAV was down 6.7% from September's level of $1.20.
At the end of last month, just over half of its portfolio was invited in direct equities including Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ), Facebook (NASDAQ: FB ) and Mastercard (NYSE: MA ), amongst others, with about 40% in cash, almost 2% in fixed income investments and 5.5% in private equity investments.
In current market conditions, the board expects that Astoria's shares will continue to trade at a discount to its NAV," Astoria said. "Following a strategic review of all options, the board has resolved to propose to unlock value for shareholders through a realisation by Astoria of all its liquid investments in order to return a substantial portion of its capital in cash to shareholders."
Earlier this year, RECM announced its firm intention to make a R13.50 per share offer to Astoria's minorities. If the level of acceptances was above the R355 million in spare cash it had, it would use a combination of cash and its own preference shares to fund the acquisition. At the time, Astoria cautioned against the offer, saying the structure could leave them shortchanged. Instead, it said it was undertaking a strategic review of its business to unlock the discount to NAV.
It now needs shareholders to vote in favour of the proposed reduction of stated capital, which will then be transferred to its non-distributable reserves. That will leave the group significantly smaller, with limited remaining capital invested in its less liquid private-equity portfolio, which may attract the interest of other third parties.
The initial amount of the capital payment will be dependent on how much cash it gets for its liquid assets and the amount of capital it needs to hold to meet Mauritian solvency requirements. At present, it doesn't expect the initial mount to exceed 84.6 US cents per share, which works out at about R12.13 at current exchange rates.
Its shares rose 1.9% to R12.86 yesterday.
